content_metadata.description: A detailed examination of a sheep brain cross-section, highlighting various anatomical structures and the flow of cerebral spinal fluid.

qAndA.question: What structure separates the two lateral ventricles?
What does the pineal gland produce?
What is the name of the tree-like white matter in the cerebellum?

qAndA.answer: The corpora quadrigemina is posterior to the thalamus.
qAndA.question: Where is the corpora quadrigemina located in relation to the thalamus?

qAndA.answer: The arbor vitae appears as a light, branching pattern compared to the darker surrounding cerebellum tissue.
qAndA.question: What visual characteristic distinguishes the arbor vitae from the surrounding cerebellum?

activities.description: Identify corpus callosum and lateral ventricles
Trace cerebral spinal fluid flow to central canal
Identify medulla oblongata, pons, and optic chiasma

characterInteraction.description: The narrator interacts with the viewer by directly addressing them and explaining the structures of the sheep brain.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Understanding the basic anatomy and fluid dynamics within the brain, relevant for educational purposes

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator identifies and follows the flow of cerebral spinal fluid through the brain, explaining structures and functions along the way starting with the corpus callosum and lateral ventricles, then moving to the third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, and finally the central canal.

scenes.thematicElements: The main theme is the anatomy of the sheep brain and the flow of cerebral spinal fluid through its ventricles.
scenes.title: Introduction and Examination

climax.description: The narrator concludes by identifying the medulla oblongata, pons, and optic chiasma.

storylines.description: The video focuses on identifying and explaining the internal structures of a sheep brain, particularly the flow of cerebral spinal fluid.

text_to_speech: Now let’s look at the cross section of the sheep brain. Once you have observed the external structures of the cerebrum and the cerebellum and the brain stem and the inferior portion of the sheep brain, you want to cut the sheep brain in half, right along that longitudinal fissure. Once you make an equal mid-sagittal plane of dissection, observe the structures. Here we can see, deep to the cerebral cortex, you have this white matter that connects the two cerebral hemispheres. This is referred to as the corpus callosum. The corpus callosum is also going to contain the lateral ventricles that are deep to it. Here going through this membrane, the septum pellucidum separates the lateral ventricles. Ventricles 1 and 2 that are going to contain cerebral spinal fluid. The lateral ventricles will then continue to flow that fluid through the choroid plexus here and around this intermediate mass. Once they go around the intermediate mass we have the 3rd ventricle. The third ventricle goes above and below the intermediate mass. This intermediate mass is where we have the thalamus. Below the thalamus we come down and there’s an approximate area here referred to as the hypothalamus. And as we saw before the hypothalamus will connect by an infundibulum to the pituitary gland. This sheep specimen does not have the pituitary gland attached. Here posterior to the corpus callosum and the thalamus we see another gland. This is the pineal gland. The pineal gland contains melatonin to regulate cyclic activity, such as sleep. Posterior to the pineal gland we also have the corpora quadrigemina. The corpora quadrigemina has four sections. Here we can see two parts: the superior colliculus and the inferior colliculus. There is one set on each side of the brain, a left and a right. Here we see the superior colliculus and the inferior colliculus. The cerebral spinal fluid that flows through the 3rd ventricle will continue on through this little channel that looks like a river-bed or groove and this is referred to as the cerebral aqueduct. The cerebral aqueduct will continue on and once we continue to move that fluid below the cerebellum we have the 4th ventricle. Here in the cerebellum cross-section we can see a beautiful tree-like structure. This white matter is referred to as the arbor vitae. The arbor vitae is going to have folia extensions near the outskirts of this cortex. As we continue on from the fourth ventricle the cerebral spinal fluid will flow into the central canal. And we can see a darkened area here appearing to be the central part of the spinal cord. Once again we can see a cross-section/medial view of the medulla oblongata and the pons. Here we can also see a medial view of the optic chiasm. This is the center for the crossing over of the optic nerves. So let’s review this again. On a different specimen we can see the corpus callosum. The septum pellucidum separates the lateral ventricles. The third ventricle goes around the thalamus. The hypothalamus is below the thalamus and connects by an infundibulum to the pituitary gland, which we see here. Here, this gland is the pineal gland, posterior to the corpus callosum and the thalamus. We can also see two sections of the corpora quadrigemina, the superior colliculus and the inferior colliculus. The third ventricle travels through the cerebral aqueduct and continues to pick up fluid joining with the fourth ventricle. This fluid continues to flow out through the central canal into the spinal cord. These tree like branches in the cerebellum are referred to as the arbor vitae. Here I can see the optic chiasm, the pons, and medulla oblongata.
